opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I come at it from the explainable AI side. For years my group has worked on feature attribution, on understanding why a model makes a particular prediction, and single-cell foundation models are a place where that matters more than ever.

What's exciting about these models is that they're trained on tens of millions of cells across many tissues, conditions, and donors, so they learn very rich representations of cell state. But a representation that performs well on cell type annotation or batch integration doesn't tell a biologist *why*. If we want these models to generate biological insight, not just good benchmark numbers, we need to be able to open them up.

I think about the challenge on a few levels.

The first is attribution at the input level: which genes drive a model's embedding of a cell or its prediction for that cell? Methods like Shapley-value-based attributions help here, but single-cell data makes them harder. Expression is sparse and noisy, genes are highly correlated because they work in programs and pathways, and the input space is huge. Naively attributing to individual genes can give unstable or misleading answers. So we've been interested in attributing to groups of genes, or to biologically meaningful units like pathways and gene programs, and in being careful about what the baseline or reference distribution is. In single-cell data the choice of reference cells really changes the answer.

The second level is understanding the internal representations. These models are often transformers, and people have been tempted to read attention weights as gene-gene interactions or regulatory relationships. I'm cautious about that. Attention isn't necessarily explanation, and we should test whether those patterns actually correspond to known biology or causal structure before treating them that way. That's where ideas from mechanistic interpretability, like finding interpretable directions or features in the latent space, become interesting, with sparse dictionary-style approaches being one example. Can we find features that correspond to a cell cycle program, an interferon response, a disease-associated state? And can we verify that?

The third level, which I think is most important, is validation. Interpretability in biology has a huge advantage over many other domains: we can do experiments. If a model says a set of genes is driving a particular cell state, we can check that against perturbation data, CRISPR screens, or independent cohorts. I'd like the field to move toward interpretability claims that are falsifiable and tested, rather than pretty pictures of attention maps.

There's also a practical point. Biologists and clinicians will only trust and use these models if they can interrogate them. If a model flags a subpopulation of cells as associated with drug resistance in a tumor, the immediate question is which genes, which pathways, and whether it's real biology or a batch artifact. Explainability is often how you catch the model learning a technical confounder rather than the signal you care about. So for me it's not an add-on. It's part of making these models scientifically useful and safe to rely on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that interpretability for these models is still an open problem, and I'd push back a little on the framing that we just need to "make them interpretable" after the fact.

My lab has spent a lot of time on explainable AI, going back to the SHAP work with Scott Lundberg, and one thing we learned is that an explanation is only useful if it connects to a question a biologist actually cares about. So when a single-cell foundation model is trained on tens of millions of cells and learns some embedding of gene expression, asking "which genes are important" in the abstract isn't that meaningful. What people want to know is something like: which regulatory programs drive this cell state, what changes when you perturb this gene, which features distinguish responders from non-responders to a drug.

So the way I think about it is in layers. First, there's the question of whether the model has even learned something real. There have been some sobering benchmark papers showing that for certain tasks, these large pretrained models don't beat simple baselines. If the representation isn't capturing biology, explaining it is explaining noise.

Second, assuming it has learned something, we need attribution methods that work at the right level of abstraction. Attributing to twenty thousand individual genes is overwhelming. Attributing to pathways, gene modules, or latent factors that have been grounded against prior knowledge, that's much closer to how a biologist reasons.

Third, and this is where I think the field is heading, is treating interpretation as a scientific tool for discovery rather than a post-hoc check. Can the model generate a hypothesis about a mechanism, and can we design an experiment to test it? That closes the loop. We've worked on this in the context of drug response and aging, where the explanation itself becomes a candidate biomarker or target that you then go validate.

The last thing I'd say is that we should be careful about anthropomorphizing. A heatmap of attention weights looks interpretable, but it's not evidence of anything until it predicts an outcome you didn't train on. Faithfulness matters more than plausibility, and those two are easy to confuse when the output looks like biology.

r002.rationale: It says abstract gene-importance attributions are not meaningful, but does not state that downstream attribution assumes individual input features are biologically interpretable units.

r003.rationale: It says pathways, gene modules, or grounded latent factors are closer to how biologists reason than attribution to individual genes.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do we mean by biologically interpretable? A model may learn a representation that is very useful for predicting cell types, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we understand what biology it has learned. Is it capturing a regulatory process, or is it capturing something about how the data were collected?

So I would start with a specific biological question. If the model predicts that a cell responds to a treatment, can we identify which genes, or which relationships among genes, drive that prediction? And then, do those explanations remain consistent across different datasets and experimental conditions?

There’s also an important distinction between explaining a prediction and discovering a mechanism. An explanation can tell us what the model relies on. It cannot, by itself, establish that changing a particular gene will cause a particular cellular response. That requires additional evidence, ideally perturbation experiments.

To me, that’s the opportunity: use interpretability to turn what these models learn into testable biological hypotheses. We should evaluate not only how accurately a model predicts, but also whether its explanations help us ask better questions and design informative experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, what do we mean by biologically interpretable? A model can learn a very useful representation of a cell, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we understand what biological information it has captured or how it uses that information to make a prediction.

For me, the challenge is connecting the model’s behavior to biological questions. If it predicts a particular cell state, which genes contributed to that prediction? Do those genes point to a coherent pathway? And does that explanation hold across different donors, experimental conditions, or datasets?

We also have to be careful about the distinction between explaining a prediction and identifying a biological mechanism. A model may rely on a gene because it is correlated with a process, not because that gene drives the process. So explanations can help us generate hypotheses, but we need perturbation experiments and other evidence to test those hypotheses.

Ultimately, I would like these models to help us understand something we didn’t already know about biology. That requires evaluating the explanations as seriously as we evaluate predictive performance.
